items.title: ‘Delhi became the source of all real knowledge’: How TV newsrooms pushed regional reporters aside
items.summary: Today, it feels as if the role of the reporter on a TV news channel has shrunk compared to the days when we started out. There are, of course, honourable exceptions, reporters who continue to produce high-quality work that makes an impact. But too many of the new crop of reporters deliver just what is expected of them—which is not enough in terms of originality and high standards. What is expected can, however, be too much in terms of working hours, number of lives or ‘OB’s. But with little reward in terms of the feeling of a responsible and important job well done, burnout is faster for the young reporter today. The initial thrill of coming on air and having access to the powerful can last a while, but is not enough to sustain them for a long career. A young reporter I worked with was very clear when she said, ‘I don’t want to be doing this when I am thirty!’ I had been on the job for more years than she had been alive, but I could understand where she was coming from. items.title: Husband and wife living in same house but different rooms not cruelty by itself: Karnataka HC
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court recently held that merely occupying separate rooms in the same premises does not, by itself, constitute matrimonial cruelty. A Bench of Justices DK Singh and H Shanthi Bhushan said that such separation can assume significance when viewed alongside the broader matrimonial history of a couple. The Court noted that the husband in this case himself had admitted that the parties had occupied separate rooms for a considerable period. “Standing by itself, such an arrangement cannot be treated as cruelty. The mere fact that spouses occupy separate rooms, without anything more, would not justify a finding of cruelty." It held that the separation could not be viewed in isolation and formed part of a prolonged matrimonial history involving repeated disputes, allegations of abuse, estrangement, an earlier matrimonial proceeding and the eventual failure of the relationship. The Court made the observation while dismissing an appeal filed by a man against a family court verdict which dissolved his marriage with his wife on the ground of cruelty and directed him to pay permanent alimony of ₹25,000 per month.
